title: Mobil Oil Corp. v. Federal Power Commission
lead: The Commission turns a cost-allocation problem into nationwide transportation rates, but its authority over liquids and its unexplored statistical foundation fail separate tests.

actors.name: Mobil Oil Corporation
actors.role: Producer challenging nationwide minimum transportation charges.

actors.name: Federal Power Commission
actors.role: Agency issuing Order 449 and defending its jurisdiction and process.

actors.name: Gas producers, pipelines, and state agencies
actors.role: Participants in comments and conferences leading to the rate order.

proceedings: The Commission proposed allocation policy, held informal conferences, and adopted minimum rates without further notice.
Mobil sought rehearing unsuccessfully and petitioned for review.
The D.C. Circuit vacated the orders and remanded on jurisdictional and independent procedural grounds.
limits: The opinion describes the court’s 1973 approach to evidentiary procedure, not a certification of current hybrid-rulemaking doctrine. It did not choose lawful rates or find every disputed cost figure false.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Mixed well output creates a risk of shifting costs to gas consumers
sections.cue: How had the Commission previously handled that risk?
paragraphs: Natural-gas wells can produce liquid petroleum, gas that later becomes liquid—liquefiables—and natural gas itself. Producers sometimes sold the gas but retained the other products, sending all through a pipeline because separation at the well was not always economical. Transporting retained products consumed capacity and imposed costs that could fall on gas consumers if their owners paid too little.

From 1954 to 1968, the Federal Power Commission addressed this through individual certificate and rate proceedings, allocating nongas transport costs away from permissible gas charges. That differed from fixing mandatory transportation prices directly for retained products.

In February 1968 the Commission proposed a general cost-allocation policy. The notice did not propose the nationwide minimum rates eventually adopted. Fifteen producers, eleven pipelines, and two state agencies commented; only the state agencies supported it. Those initial submissions lacked the cost data later used to set the minimums.

sources.pinpoint: Transportation problem and change; 483 F.2d at 1241–44 & nn.3–4

sections.title: Settlement figures enter informal conferences and become a national rate basis
sections.cue: What opportunity existed to test the data?
paragraphs: About two and a half years later, a Commission lawyer conducted a September 29, 1970 conference without a transcript; paraphrased minutes recorded it. Staff sought facts, but participants deferred further work pending a Southern Louisiana settlement. At an October conference, pipeline counsel supplied nine sheets of cost-of-service figures prepared for that settlement. They had not been sponsored as evidence, cross-examined, or met with contrary proof and were not prepared for this nationwide rule. Later conferences were again deferred.

Without another notice or conference, the Commission issued Order 449 on January 31, 1972. It declared cost allocation inadequate without explaining why the former approach no longer protected gas consumers and prescribed minimum transportation charges: two cents per Mcf per hundred miles for liquefiables and twenty cents per barrel for liquids. The regulation applied the conditions to covered contractual and certificate arrangements.

Mobil unsuccessfully sought rehearing and then judicial review, challenging jurisdiction, settlement privilege, procedure, evidentiary support, and discrimination or preference. The court rejected privilege because, under the Commission’s previously sustained interpretation, protection belonged to the offeror and Mobil was not the offeror. That did not establish the data as a valid evidentiary foundation. The inadequate record prevented a separate resolution of discrimination.

sources.pinpoint: Conferences, order, and challenges; 483 F.2d at 1244–46 & nn.7–13

sections.title: Wilkey finds no statutory authority to set liquid-petroleum transport prices
sections.cue: Why was protection of gas consumers not enough?
paragraphs: Judge Wilkey’s opinion began with the Natural Gas Act’s coverage of natural gas rather than liquid petroleum. The Commission argued that liquids formed part of a regulated larger transaction and that minimum payments prevented gas consumers from subsidizing producers. Neither supplied power to regulate an excluded product. Precedents involving gas production, extraction, and pipelines did not expand the statutory definition; Congress had to grant the additional authority.

The Commission also had not shown why cost allocation failed or direct liquid pricing was indispensable. Nongas costs could be excluded from gas charges without regulating the nongas service itself. The court set aside liquid-price provisions for want of jurisdiction. Jurisdiction over liquefiables was uncontested, but their rates still required review of the process and evidence.

sections.title: The court rejects automatic formal hearings but insists on an adequate factual record
sections.cue: Which sources of authority did the agency invoke?
paragraphs: Mobil could not demand every incident of formal rulemaking under Administrative Procedure Act §§ 556 and 557. The Natural Gas Act lacked the required on-the-record direction, and its legislative history did not supply that intent. United States v. Florida East Coast Railway controlled that issue.

The court nonetheless rejected a choice limited to either a full trial or wholly untested comments. In its historical approach, intermediate devices—written questions, screening, and limited cross-examination—could test disputed facts without unrestricted oral examination. This was an interpretation of this statute’s evidentiary requirements, not a declaration that all informal rulemaking needed those devices.

Section 16’s necessary-or-appropriate authority implemented existing substantive powers; it neither created new jurisdiction nor erased safeguards. Permian Basin’s approval of practical area-rate regulation did not allow fixed rates based on untested facts, and an earlier Mobil case sustaining a jurisdiction-preserving moratorium did not validate this actual rate decision.

The Natural Gas Act required substantial evidence on the whole record, including contrary material. Although the Attorney General’s manual associated that standard with formal proceedings, the court did not infer all formal hearing procedures. It required meaningful development and testing of the essential factual predicates under the statute.

sources.pinpoint: Formal procedures; Section 16 and review; 483 F.2d at 1249–59 & n.68

sections.title: The nine sheets do not establish a reliable national rate foundation
sections.cue: Why did another proceeding’s fuller record not cure the omission?
paragraphs: The Commission used material without warning participants that it would support national rates and without adequate rebuttal opportunity. The figures covered only ten of 116 pipelines, with no showing of representativeness, and used differing test years. The missing record also prevented effective judicial appraisal of claims that expenses were overstated. A fuller record in Southern Louisiana was not the record developed here.

Florida East Coast Railway did not answer this separate evidentiary problem because its Interstate Commerce Commission proceeding lacked the same congressional substantial-evidence requirement. The panel also rejected the Tenth Circuit Phillips majority’s reasoning in favor of Judge Seth’s dissent there. That comparative dissent belonged to another case, not to this panel.

At argument the Commission acknowledged that later individual proceedings had found nine of the ten pipelines’ cost figures too high. That discrepancy reinforced the need to examine evidence before applying it nationally, without establishing that every figure or all potential rates were false.

sources.pinpoint: Why record failed; Remand discussion; 483 F.2d at 1259–63 & nn.78–79, 93

sections.title: The remand requires a justified policy choice and a testable record
sections.cue: What options remained for the Commission?
paragraphs: Participants had to be able to test factual predicates and place relevant evidence in a reviewable record. Full formal procedures would suffice but were unnecessary; written questions or screened and limited oral examination might work, and a transcript could cure inadequate conference minutes. The court described alternatives rather than one invariable hearing design.

Evidence from another proceeding could be incorporated if the relevant evidence itself—not merely agency conclusions or untested settlement terms—had been tested and affected parties received notice and a chance to comment. The Commission first had to explain why mandatory liquefiables charges were needed instead of cost allocation, then justify any lawful rate on an adequate record.

The court vacated the challenged orders and remanded. It stressed that lack of fair notice and record support independently required remand even if broader jurisdictional or procedural reasoning were rejected. Wilkey wrote for Judges Leventhal and Senior District Judge Jameson without separate opinions; the decision issued July 11, 1973 and was amended July 26.

The assigned later discussion of burdens from such intermediate hearing requirements and Vermont Yankee’s response is editorial history. Vermont Yankee’s own excerpt is a different decision. This account preserves Mobil’s historical reasoning without presenting that procedural approach as certified current law or supplying a later rate outcome.

sources.pinpoint: Remand and historical limits; 483 F.2d at 1238, 1262–64 & nn.91–95
